articles.title: An Ohio community is negotiating to buy 850 acres from a coal company; if successful, the public forest could link about 74,000 acres between Wayne National Forest and Strouds Run State Park
articles.summary: US News: An effort in southeast Ohio could turn roughly 850 acres of former coal-company land into a publicly accessible community forest, creating a major con.
articles.body: An effort in southeast Ohio could turn roughly 850 acres of former coal-company land into a publicly accessible community forest, creating a major connection between existing protected and recreational lands. Local stakeholders are negotiating with the Sugar Creek Coal and Mining Company to acquire the property in Dover Township and establish the Sugar Creek Community Forest. The project could ultimately link the Bailey’s portion of Wayne National Forest with Strouds Run State Park, connecting about 74,000 acres in Athens County. The details come from the announcement for the upcoming Sugar Creek Community Forest town hall, alongside information published by the Ohio Environmental Council and project partners.From coal-company land to a community forestThe proposed acquisition involves approximately 850 acres in Dover Township that are currently owned by the Sugar Creek Coal and Mining Company. Local stakeholders are working to purchase the land and establish it as the Sugar Creek Community Forest, with the intention that it remains available for community benefit in perpetuity.The proposal is part of a broader effort involving Rising Appalachia and other community, environmental and regional partners. The Ohio Environmental Council describes the project as an attempt to develop a regenerative conservation and economic model in Appalachian Ohio, bringing together nonprofits, foundations, educational institutions, businesses, government officials and local residents. The land has significance beyond its size. It sits in a location where conservation of the property could create a continuous corridor between several existing public and conservation landscapes.A potential 74,000-acre connectionOne of the most important aspects of the proposal is its potential role as a connector. According to the community announcement, the property is positioned to create a publicly accessible biodiversity, recreation and wildlife corridor linking the Bailey’s portion of the Wayne National Forest with Strouds Run State Park. The resulting connected landscape could encompass about 74,000 acres in Athens County.Earlier, the Ohio Environmental Council described a roughly 900-acre vision that would connect about 75,000 acres of state, federal and private conservation lands. The Trust for Public Land, which is now involved in the project, describes the current effort as protecting more than 845 acres and connecting the community forest to a broader network of trails and public land. The connection could have implications for both people and wildlife. Rather than leaving forests and recreation areas separated by privately held parcels, a community forest could provide a link through which people can move between existing trail and conservation networks while helping maintain habitat connectivity.Public recreation and rural traditionsThe proposed forest is intended to be more than a protected tract of woodland. The community announcement says the land could support recreation, biodiversity and wildlife while preserving rural activities such as hunting, foraging and gathering firewood. Similarly, the Trust for Public Land states the project intends to provide residents access to activities including hunting, fishing, foraging and firewood gathering. Its description of the project also includes plans connected to education, sustainable tourism, forest-based businesses and workforce development.That community-use element is central to the idea of a community forest. The Ohio Environmental Council says the Sugar Creek project is grounded in regenerative land management, community input and culturally appropriate economic opportunities. It has also described the initiative as a potential model for community-governed land use in Ohio.Restoring a landscape shaped by coal miningThe proposal also carries a larger environmental-recovery story. The Sugar Creek property is part of a landscape historically affected by coal mining, and the wider Sunday Creek watershed has faced environmental damage associated with mining. Earlier reporting on the project noted that the Sugar Creek Coal Company ceased mining the property in 1923, while parts of the land have subsequently experienced logging. Rising Appalachia has sought to protect the remaining forest from being divided, logged and developed.Restoration is therefore another major component of the proposed community forest. The project specifically identifies continued ecological restoration of the Sunday Creek Watershed as one of the potential benefits of conserving the property. The project is also connected to work already taking place at Solid Ground Farm, where Rising Appalachia has developed ecological education, workforce training and land-based initiatives. The Ohio Environmental Council says its partnership with Rising Appalachia has included an ecology apprenticeship programme, native fruit and nut plantings and an interpretive trail on former coal-mined land.An economic opportunity as well as a conservation projectSupporters see the forest as a potential economic asset for the surrounding community rather than simply a conservation purchase. The community announcement identifies opportunities for local entrepreneurs in land-based food, construction and recreation businesses. The broader project vision also includes sustainable timber and forest products, educational activities and recreation-related enterprises. This approach reflects a larger idea behind the project: that restoring forests and waterways can happen alongside efforts to create livelihoods.For now, however, the proposed forest remains dependent on completing the land acquisition. Local stakeholders are continuing to work towards securing the property and involving residents in decisions about its future. A community town hall is scheduled for September 28 in Chauncey, where residents are being invited to learn more about the proposed Sugar Creek Community Forest and participate in the discussion about what the land could become.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Saudi Arabia reports 110 million tonnes of ore containing uranium and heavy rare earths in Madinah, boosting its nuclear and mining ambitions
articles.summary: Middle East News: A large mineral resource reported in western Saudi Arabia has added another piece to the kingdom’s expanding plans for critical minerals and nuclear e.
articles.body: A large mineral resource reported in western Saudi Arabia has added another piece to the kingdom’s expanding plans for critical minerals and nuclear energy. Exploration at Jabal Sayid in the Madinah region has identified an estimated 110 million tonnes of ore containing high concentrations of rare earth elements, particularly heavier varieties, as well as uranium, according to Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, according to the X post (Formerly Twitter). The announcement was made at the International Atomic Energy Agency’s General Conference in Vienna on September 14. The figure refers to the estimated ore resource, rather than 110 million tonnes of rare earths or uranium themselves.What lies inside Saudi Arabia’s 110 million tonne mineral resourceThe reported discovery comes from exploration and geological work carried out around Jabal Sayid, an area already attracting attention for its mineral potential. The newly disclosed estimate covers about 110 million tonnes of ore in which rare earth elements occur alongside uranium.The rare earth component is particularly significant because the deposit contains heavier rare earth elements. These include minerals such as dysprosium and terbium, which are used in specialised technologies and high-performance magnets. Lighter elements including neodymium and praseodymium are also associated with the wider resource.The ministry’s announcement did not mean that all 110 million tonnes could be extracted as commercially usable rare earth material. The number describes the estimated quantity of ore identified through exploration, while the concentrations of the individual elements determine what could ultimately be recovered.Saudi Arabia’s Jabal Sayid holds large rare earth and uranium resourcesJabal Sayid is not a new name in Saudi Arabia’s mining plans. The site, about 350 kilometres north-east of Jeddah, has previously been identified as one of the country’s important rare earth prospects.An analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, drawing on estimates from Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources and state mining company Maaden, put the site’s heavy rare earth resources at around 552,000 tonnes. A further 355,000 tonnes were estimated to consist of lighter rare earth elements.Those figures place the deposit among the larger known rare earth resources globally, according to the analysis. Heavy rare earths such as dysprosium and terbium are of particular interest because supplies are concentrated in relatively few parts of the world.The site also has a uranium component. The same analysis estimated a co-located uranium resource of about 31,000 tonnes. That combination gives Jabal Sayid a different significance from a conventional rare earth project. It potentially links mineral extraction with Saudi Arabia’s longer-term interest in producing nuclear fuel.Saudi Arabia explores a domestic route to nuclear fuelSaudi Arabia has been developing plans for a civilian nuclear programme while seeking greater control over the resources and industrial capacity needed to support it. The latest announcement comes less than two months after Washington and Riyadh formalised a civil nuclear cooperation agreement. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Prince Abdulaziz signed the deal on July 22, establishing a framework for long-term cooperation in civilian nuclear energy, according to the US Department of Energy.The US Department of Energy described the agreements as providing a legal basis for a multibillion-dollar partnership lasting decades. They are also intended to give US companies greater access to Saudi Arabia’s civilian nuclear programme.Against that background, a domestic uranium resource has an obvious relevance. A resource inside the kingdom could form part of efforts to develop a local nuclear fuel supply chain, although the existence of an identified resource does not by itself mean that commercial uranium production is ready to begin.There are still technical, economic and regulatory stages between geological identification and actual mining.Rare earth ambitions grew after the 2025 US visitThe mineral announcement also fits into a broader push that has accelerated since Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to the United States in November 2025. During that period, Saudi Arabia and the US expanded cooperation around critical minerals, metals and supply chains. Maaden, Saudi Arabia’s state-backed mining company, also entered into a partnership with US-based MP Materials, the company behind the United States’ only rare earth mine and processing operation. A Strategic Framework for Cooperation followed, covering critical minerals and uranium among other areas.Under the arrangement, the US Department of Defense agreed to finance 49% of a planned rare earth processing plant in Saudi Arabia. Maaden is expected to hold the remaining 51% alongside MP Materials, as reported by The Arab News. The arrangement reflects a wider attempt to develop mineral processing capacity closer to the countries seeking to secure supplies of materials considered strategically important.For Saudi Arabia, the objective is not limited to identifying deposits. Processing and refining are equally important because extracting ore is only one part of turning a geological resource into a usable industrial material.Saudi Arabia says its rare earth resources are growingThe Jabal Sayid announcement follows other large resource estimates reported by Saudi authorities. The Saudi Press Agency reported in November 2025 that the value attributed to the kingdom’s rare earth discoveries had reached $100 billion. It described that figure as a 90% increase compared with 2018.Separate work by the Saudi Geological Survey has identified two advanced exploration areas containing an estimated 644 million tonnes of resources. These numbers form part of Saudi Arabia’s attempt to expand mining beyond its historically important commodities and make greater use of the geological resources spread across the kingdom.Rare earth elements are particularly relevant because they are used across industries ranging from electronics and renewable energy equipment to electric motors and defence-related technologies. Their supply chains have also become an important area of international competition.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt rushed to Buffalo by train after McKinley died and took office in a friend's library; 125 years later, it is reenacted in the same room
articles.summary: US News: On September 14, 1901, Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Buffalo after President William McKinley died from injuries suffered in an assassination attempt..
articles.body: On September 14, 1901, Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Buffalo after President William McKinley died from injuries suffered in an assassination attempt. Roosevelt reached the city at 1.30pm and was taken to the home of Ansley Wilcox, a friend who would soon provide the setting for an unexpected presidential inauguration.According to Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site, Roosevelt first went to the home of John Milburn, where McKinley had been staying, to pay his respects to Mrs McKinley. He then returned to the Wilcox home. There, the library was chosen as the place for him to take the oath of office as the 26th president of the United States.The ceremony took place at about 3.30pm, only hours after McKinley's death. A small group was present, including a few newspaper reporters who were allowed to take notes. Photographers were kept out of the room until after the ceremony. Roosevelt also wore formal clothes borrowed from some of the guests who were there.Federal District Judge John R. Hazel administered the oath. Immediately after becoming president, Roosevelt held a short Cabinet meeting in the same library. He then went to the morning room to issue his first presidential proclamation.The room where that ceremony took place is now part of the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site in Buffalo. On the 125th anniversary of Roosevelt's unexpected inauguration, the site is brought the event back to the same library with a live reenactment.Reenactment on September 14The Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural Site hosted the reenactment on September 14, 2026. The event featured Joe Wiegand, a performer known for portraying Roosevelt.The organisers say the reenactment took place in the very room where Roosevelt took the presidential oath in 1901. Wiegand followed part of the same journey that Roosevelt made more than a century ago. He arrived in Buffalo by train on the afternoon of September 14.According to the event organisers, “TR” was expected to arrive downtown at about 3:45pm, depending on the arrival time of the Amtrak train. He then traveled to the historic Ansley Wilcox House and prepared to take the oath.The reenactment began at 4:30pm. It recreated the moment when Roosevelt formally became president after McKinley's death.The event was presented as an opportunity for visitors to experience the historic ceremony in the place where it happened. The organisers described it as a chance to imagine being “IN the room where it happened”.The 35-word oath repeatedDuring the reenactment, Wiegand delivered the 35-word presidential oath that Roosevelt spoke in 1901. He raised his hand and take the oath in the same library.The National Park Service records that Roosevelt had selected the Wilcox library as the most appropriate location for the ceremony. After the oath, he stayed there for a Cabinet meeting before moving to another room to issue his first presidential proclamation.Event livestreamedThe September 14 reenactment was livestreamed through the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural Site's social media platforms. However, only a limited number of people were able to watch the event from inside the library.VIP tickets were sold for those who want exclusive access to the live reenactment. The organisers said proceeds will benefit the site's civic education programming.The VIP ticket costed $500 per person or $850 per couple. The ticket also includes access to the site's Exemplary Citizenship Reception scheduled for 6pm on September 15, the following evening. Tickets for the Double-Decker Bus Tour are not included and have to be purchased separately.The Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site is located at 641 Delaware Avenue in Buffalo, New York. The site is operated by the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural Site Foundation through a cooperative agreement with the National Park Service.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Once again surrendering to US pressure': Rahul slams govt over UPI fee exemption limit
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul on Tuesday accused the Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led government of “surrendering to pressure from American corpora.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul on Tuesday accused the Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led government of “surrendering to pressure from American corporations” by reportedly paving the way for charges on certain Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions.Rahul argued that although the government has said consumers will not be charged directly, allowing a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on merchant transactions above Rs 2,000 could eventually lead to higher retail prices.Sharing a post on X, the leader of opposition said, "The Modi government has quietly opened the door to imposing fees on UPI. Now, MDR can be levied on merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000. Even if these transactions account for just 5% of the volume, they make up nearly 65% of UPI's total transaction value.""The government says no fees will be charged to customers. But where will the fees imposed on shopkeepers ultimately come from? Added to prices, straight out of the customer's pocket. American payment companies have long opposed India's zero-MDR policy. Now, the Modi government has opened the path to changing the policy in exactly that direction. Just like with the US Trade Deal, Compromised PM Modi is once again surrendering to American pressure," he added.Rahul’s remarks came after the government directed banks and payment system providersnot to impose direct or indirect charges on UPI transactions of up to Rs 2,000or on payments made through RuPay debit cards.However, the notification does not clarify whether charges could be imposed on transactions above Rs 2,000, particularly those made by merchants. UPI transactions have so far remained free of charges, irrespective of the amount.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge also accused the PM Modi government of laying the groundwork for a “Digital Payments Tax” by allowing the possibility of charges on UPI transactions above Rs 2,000.“The Modi government's loot has now reached UPI. "No fees on UPI" has been changed to "no fees on UPI transactions up to Rs 2,000." Sky-high inflation has already emptied the common man's pocket. Wholesale inflation is near 10%, and the BJP government has planned to impose a "Digital Payments Tax" on the public, aiming to destroy whatever little savings they have left,” Kharge said in an X post.“Ten years ago, demonetization delivered a shock to the country's economy. When questions were raised about the disastrous outcomes of demonetization, the government argued that it was imposed to promote Digital Payments and a Cashless Economy. The Finance Minister had recently stated in Parliament that no Tax or Charges would be levied on UPI, but according to several reports: A potential collection of Rs 25 on a Rs 5,000 transaction and up to Rs 50 on Rs 10,000. Is this true?” he added.He also warned that any Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) imposed on merchants could eventually be passed on to consumers through higher prices.Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh also questioned whether the transaction limit could be changed through a future notification to cover person-to-person transfers.“It is evident that the groundwork is being laid to collect fees on UPI transactions from all of us. Tomorrow, through another similar notification, this limit could also be altered—there is now no guarantee of this in the law. As far as we know, the government could impose charges even on everyday person-to-person UPI transactions,” he wrote on X. “Is all this being done with the intent of opening up digital payments for American companies to please President Trump?” he asked.What does the notification say?According to a gazette notification dated September 14, no bank or system provider can impose a direct or indirect charge on a person making or receiving a payment through a RuPay debit card or a UPI transaction of up to Rs 2,000.The notification follows an amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The amendment provides an enabling framework for imposing MDR on UPI and other notified electronic payment modes.The amendment Bill was passed by Parliament during the Monsoon Session, which concluded on August 13, 2026. The government had said that the UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), would decide the MDR rates.The government has argued that rising transaction volumes require continuous investment in cybersecurity, fraud prevention and payment infrastructure. It has also said that charges would support market expansion, encourage competition and help create a self-sustaining revenue model for the payments ecosystem.UPI is operated by NPCI, an initiative of the Reserve Bank of India and the Indian Banks’ Association. It enables real-time payments between individuals and allows customers to pay merchants directly.Launched on August 25, 2016, UPI has transformed India’s digital payments landscape. Its transaction value rose from Rs 0.07 lakh crore in FY17 to around Rs 314 lakh crore in FY26, an increase of more than 4,000 times in a decade.UPI is now accepted in 11 countries, including Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, Greece and Uzbekistan.According to Reuters, the introduction of UPI charges could benefit Paytm and Pine Labs, create an additional revenue stream for banks and improve prospects for IPO-bound PhonePe and Razorpay. Analysts at Jefferies estimate that the fees could generate Rs 5,000 crore to Rs 10,000 crore annually for the payments industry.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Fake cancer drugs and ICU injections sold at 50% off, and hospitals bought them
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Special Investigation Team (SIT) probe into a suspected fake-drug network in Bengaluru has raised a question that goes well beyond one .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Special Investigation Team (SIT) probe into a suspected fake-drug network in Bengaluru has raised a question that goes well beyond one pharmacy or one city: how easily can spurious or diverted medicines enter India’s legitimate healthcare system? The SIT has traced suspected spurious and mislabelled medicines to more than 90 hospitals and clinics in Bengaluru and nearby areas. At the centre of the probe is a licensed pharmacist, who investigators allege used a legitimate pharmaceutical business to build a wider distribution network.Bengaluru case exposes gaps beyond the pharmacy counterInvestigators allege that the network supplied spurious and mislabelled medicines, including counterfeit versions of high-demand Pfizer products, as well as cancer drugs and ICU injections. The medicines were reportedly sold at discounts of up to 50%, making them attractive in a market where some cancer medicines can cost tens of thousands of rupees. Investigators have also found evidence of a wider operation involving more than 15 medical representatives, with supplies allegedly reaching Maharashtra and Gujarat. The investigation began after a raid on a secret stockhouse in Tavarekere, Magadi, exposed the network.The number that stands out is 90. But the more important question is what happened after these medicines reached the hospitals and clinics. Were they administered to patients? How many vials or batches were involved? Did hospitals verify where the medicines had come from? Were batch numbers checked against manufacturer records? These are critical questions because a counterfeit medicine does not necessarily enter the system through an obviously illegal channel. By the time it reaches a hospital, it can come with invoices, packaging, a pharmacist's licence and what appears to be a perfectly legitimate supply chain.Delhi points to an interstate trailBengaluru is not the only city where cancer medicines have become part of a larger investigation. In August, Delhi Police busted a multi-state racket involving the illegal trade in cancer medicines and arrested 17 people. Investigators alleged that the network dealt in stolen and counterfeit cancer drugs and that some medicines had been diverted from government hospitals before being pushed into the black market. The investigation spread across several states, suggesting that the problem may involve organised networks rather than isolated cases of fraud at the retail level.The Delhi case makes the Bengaluru investigation more significant because both point towards vulnerabilities that can exist between the manufacturer and the patient. Medicines pass through distributors, wholesalers, pharmacies and hospital procurement systems, with multiple points at which a product can be diverted, replaced or mislabelled. If drugs meant to reach patients through government hospitals can be diverted into a black-market network, the issue is no longer just about counterfeit medicines. It is also about the loss of public money and the failure of a system intended to provide treatment to patients who may not be able to afford it otherwise.Rajasthan raises a troubling questionThe Delhi investigation has also raised questions in Rajasthan after cancer-drug vials were reportedly traced to the government supply chain and a government hospital in Bikaner. The hospital has denied any role in diversion and said its records account for the medicines it received through Rajasthan Medical Services Corporation Ltd, which supplies medicines free of cost to government hospitals. The state has since ordered scrutiny of the supply chain.Put together, the Bengaluru, Delhi and Rajasthan cases point to a problem that goes beyond the manufacture of poor-quality medicines. It is also about what happens to a drug after it leaves the factory. India has more than 10,000 pharmaceutical manufacturing units and roughly a million pharmacies, making monitoring the entire chain a formidable task. Since late 2022, regulators have conducted more than 960 risk-based inspections of pharmaceutical facilities and taken around 860 enforcement actions, according to government data.Can technology stop the next fake-drug racket?India has been moving towards greater use of digital traceability, barcode systems and risk-based inspections to identify poor-quality and spurious medicines. But technology can only work if every link in the chain uses it properly. A medicine may have a genuine-looking label and packaging, but the real test is whether its journey can be independently verified from manufacturer to distributor, hospital and, ultimately, the patient.That is why the Bengaluru investigation deserves attention beyond the city. If the SIT establishes that suspected counterfeit medicines reached 90 hospitals, investigators will need to determine not only who supplied them but also where the system failed to stop them. The same questions need to be asked in Delhi, Rajasthan, Mumbai, Hyderabad and other major healthcare markets. For a patient undergoing cancer treatment, the authenticity of a drug is not a technical detail. It is fundamental to whether the treatment they paid for, or received through a government programme, is actually the treatment they were supposed to get.

articles.title: Texas landowners are suing to stop border work through Big Bend under a $46 billion federal push; the 500-mile region has historically accounted for about 1% of arrests
articles.summary: US News: Texas landowners, ranchers and business owners are taking legal action to stop the Trump administration from building border walls and related infrast.
articles.body: Texas landowners, ranchers and business owners are taking legal action to stop the Trump administration from building border walls and related infrastructure through the remote Big Bend region, arguing that the area does not face the high levels of illegal crossings used to justify the construction. The Associated Press and ABC News reported that the lawsuit was filed by Conserve Big Bend, a nonprofit focused on protecting the region’s landscape and heritage, along with six landowners, with dozens of others living along the border supporting the legal challenge. The case comes as the Trump administration pushes ahead with a $46 billion effort to secure the roughly 2,000-mile US-Mexico border. The plan includes 30-foot steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology intended to prevent migrants and smugglers from crossing into the country.In Texas, the border project has faced resistance from landowners, environmental groups, local officials, sheriffs and tourism operators. Critics say the planned infrastructure could damage private property while also affecting the region’s distinctive environmental and cultural landscape.David Keller, an archaeologist and historian who specialises in the Big Bend and lives in the region, said at a press conference in Marfa announcing the lawsuit, as reported by the Associated Press, that residents were determined to protect the place they call home. “For us, the Big Bend is not an empty place on the map,” Keller said. “It is our home.”Why landowners are challenging the border projectA central argument in the lawsuit is that the federal government is wrongly describing Big Bend as an area experiencing high levels of illegal border crossings. The Big Bend region stretches for roughly 500 miles along the US-Mexico border, representing about a quarter of the entire southern border. Yet historical Customs and Border Protection statistics cited in the lawsuit show that the region has accounted for only about 1% of border arrests.The plaintiffs argue that those figures undermine the administration’s justification for using special powers to accelerate construction. The Department of Homeland Security has relied on congressional authority that allows the secretary to waive certain environmental, archaeological and wildlife protections when officials determine that urgent border security needs require it.The legal challenge also comes as arrests along the border have fallen sharply since President Donald Trump returned to office. Laura Allen, whose family ranch could be divided by the proposed border wall, is a former county judge and a two-time Trump voter. Speaking at the press conference, she acknowledged the administration’s border-security efforts while urging officials to reconsider construction in the region.Concerns over Big Bend National ParkSome of the strongest opposition has centred on Big Bend National Park, a remote national park in southwestern Texas where the Rio Grande forms the international boundary with Mexico. The park is known for its rugged terrain, limestone canyons, desert landscape and exceptionally dark skies, drawing visitors from across the world.The government has said in court proceedings that no final construction plan has been settled for the park. Proposals made public so far have included a new road, detection technology and barriers designed to prevent vehicles from crossing the border.In August, reports that bulldozers had begun clearing land inside the park triggered widespread criticism. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott subsequently ordered a temporary pause on construction-related activity there. Opponents say a broader review is needed because the effects of border infrastructure could extend well beyond the immediate construction zone.Native American groups have warned that construction could interfere with religious practices and damage culturally significant sites. Environmental groups have raised concerns that walls and other barriers could alter natural drainage, contribute to flooding and disrupt wildlife migration. Landowners along the Rio Grande face another practical concern: access to the river. Many ranchers rely on the waterway to provide water for livestock and support agricultural activities. They say new barriers could make it difficult or impossible to reach the river from their property.For residents of Big Bend, the lawsuit is therefore about more than stopping a wall. They argue that border-security infrastructure should take into account the region’s low historical crossing numbers, fragile environment, cultural heritage and the people whose land and livelihoods could be directly affected.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Satellites, missiles or something else? US admits it has 'on-orbit' weapons for first time
articles.summary: International News: The United States has publicly acknowledged for the first time that it has weapons deployed in orbit, revealing a previously undisclosed capability. U.
articles.body: The United States has publicly acknowledged for the first time that it has weapons deployed in orbit, revealing a previously undisclosed capability. US secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said on Monday that the US now had “on-orbit space control weapons” capable of defending American forces against hostile action. Speaking at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in Maryland, Meink declined to identify the weapon or disclose when it was deployed, but said the wording of his announcement had been carefully chosen to send a deterrent message to adversaries.“This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said. He later told reporters that revealing more about the capability would undermine its deterrent value.US confirms orbital weapons but keeps details secretMeink repeatedly refused to say whether the weapon had been tested, what type of system it was or what targets it could engage. “Not going to go into specifics on the type of weapon,” he said at a press roundtable, according to The War Zone (TWZ).The US Space Force subsequently provided a broader description of the capability, saying “space control” covers missions intended to contest and control the space domain through both kinetic and non-kinetic means.Such capabilities can disrupt, degrade or, if necessary, destroy an adversary’s space systems, the Space Force said. They can be used for both offensive and defensive purposes and include systems that could interfere with satellites without physically destroying them.That has fuelled speculation about what the newly acknowledged weapon actually is. Victoria Samson of the Secure World Foundation told Financial Times that it could be a space-based jammer, noting that the US has generally sought to avoid kinetic attacks that could generate dangerous orbital debris.Clayton Swope of the Center for Strategic and International Studies, however, said Meink’s announcement was too vague to provide a clear deterrent. For an adversary such as China or Russia to understand the threat, he said, it would need at least a broad idea of the weapon’s destructive potential and what actions could trigger its use.Golden Dome adds urgency to US space pushThe disclosure comes as the Trump administration expands US military capabilities in space and develops its proposed “Golden Dome” missile defence system.Meink said the US now had “flight-ready hardware” for space-based interceptors, a key component of Golden Dome that is intended to destroy incoming missiles while they are still in space.The growing focus on orbital warfare reflects the increasing dependence of modern militaries on satellites for communications, surveillance, navigation and targeting. The US Space Force has warned that China is developing and operating space and counterspace capabilities as part of its military modernisation, while Russia regards space as a warfighting domain and considers control of space crucial to future conflicts.The US has also become more explicit about offensive space capabilities. In 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order reinforcing the Space Force’s role in protecting US assets as well as developing capabilities to attack adversary systems.Russia and China expand counterspace capabilitiesThe US disclosure comes amid growing evidence of military activity targeting satellites.In 2024, Washington said Russia had launched a satellite that it believed could be capable of attacking other spacecraft. More recently, reports indicated that two Russian satellites had potentially intercepted communications from at least a dozen European satellites since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.China has also invested heavily in counterspace technologies designed to disrupt or disable an adversary’s satellites.The development raises concerns that the US acknowledgement could accelerate an already emerging arms race in orbit. Samson warned that the disclosure could ultimately “backfire as a deterrent” if China or Russia responded by publicly acknowledging comparable weapons.Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, countries are prohibited from placing weapons of mass destruction in orbit. However, the treaty does not impose a blanket ban on conventional weapons or systems designed to interfere with or attack satellites.The US Space Force said its operations would comply with international law, including the Outer Space Treaty and the law of armed conflict.Meink, meanwhile, framed the new capability as necessary to ensure the US could continue operating freely in an increasingly contested domain.“It is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air, but in space,” he said.

articles.title: ‘Will show reality’: CJP’s Saurabh Das brings ‘School Theek Karo’ to Noida, urges youth to inspect schools
articles.summary: NOIDA: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Tuesday took its ‘School Theek Karo’ campaign to Noida, with party spokesperson Saurabh Das announcing an au.
articles.body: NOIDA: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Tuesday took its ‘School Theek Karo’ campaign to Noida, with party spokesperson Saurabh Das announcing an audit of schools in the city and urging young people across Uttar Pradesh to inspect institutions in their own neighbourhoods.Das said the team would visit schools in Noida to assess the conditions in which children are studying and document the findings.He said Noida was considered one of the better districts in Uttar Pradesh and that the team would assess whether its schools matched that perception."Today, we’ve come to Noida. We’re going to audit some schools here as part of our 'School Theek Karo' campaign. We’ll see the conditions in which children are studying. Noida is one of the better districts in UP, so hopefully, the school conditions will be good too. Whatever the situation is, we’ll show you the reality."The CJP spokesperson also appealed to young people in Uttar Pradesh to take up school audits in their respective areas and document the conditions of schools and the education being provided to children."We want young people from UP to go out and audit schools as well—to show what condition the schools in their neighbourhoods are in and what kind of education children are receiving. Today, we’re planning to visit schools in Noida, but we’d encourage other young people to take on this responsibility too and audit schools in their own areas..." Das said.CJP’s ‘School Theek Karo’ campaignThe CJP had launched its nationwide ‘School Theek Karo’ campaign in August, describing it as a social-audit drive focused on government schools and basic facilities.The campaign calls on citizens and volunteers to inspect schools and document issues related to infrastructure and essential amenities.The campaign’s first audit was conducted at a government school in Santuk Pimpri village of Maharashtra’s Hingoli district, where CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke highlighted issues including lack of drinking water, benches, dirty washrooms, broken windows and inadequate water supply.Subsequent CJP audits have also focused on classrooms, drinking-water facilities, toilets, benches and material used for preparing midday meals.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news. articles.title: In 2024, this woman spent a night inside the real Conjuring House, the 1736 Rhode Island farmhouse where the Perron family reported horrifying experiences
articles.summary: US News: If you ask a horror-movie lover about their favourite film, chances are The Conjuring series would be high on the list. And for a fan of the franchise.
articles.body: If you ask a horror-movie lover about their favourite film, chances are The Conjuring series would be high on the list. And for a fan of the franchise, getting the chance to spend a night inside the real house that inspired the story would be nothing short of a dream come true. That’s exactly what happened with creator Lux Blair (@bat.wings). One memorable stay involved spending a night inside a nearly 300-year-old farmhouse in Rhode Island, the very house that inspired the horror flick.She took to Instagram to share videos from inside the house, giving her followers a glimpse of her experience. What she encountered there, however, was something she could hardly have imagined and would want to remember ever after getting out of the house.The incidentLux Blair recently revisited the experience of staying inside the famous centuries-old house taking her followers back to the infamous property and sharing memories of staying at what is popularly known as the real Conjuring House. Her post draws attention to paranormal tourism.On one of the slides, she sums up her experience:“Maybe it was history. Maybe it was the stories. Or maybe there was something else in that house that didn’t want me there. Either way, when the morning finally came, I was more than ready to leave.”History of the houseThe house is real and is located at 1677 Round Top Road in Harrisville. It’s a village in Burrillville, Rhode Island. The property is historically known as the Old Arnold Estate. The original farmhouse was built in 1736 and stood at the centre of a working farm.Its history stretches back through generations of families, with the estate once covering roughly 200 acres. Today, the surviving farmhouse remains an extraordinary piece of colonial New England architecture, and one of the world's most famous addresses for horror fans.Perron family paranormal experiencesThe property became internationally (in) famous because of the Perron family. They moved into the farmhouse in January 1971. Roger and Carolyn Perron lived there with their five daughters named Andrea, Nancy, Christine, Cindy and April. They lived in the house until 1980. As per the family, they had strange and unexplained experiences inside the house. Over the years, these stories attracted the attention of paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren. Their story eventually inspired the 2013 Hollywood film The Conjuring.In another slide, she explains her experience, “I have read Andrea Perron’s books on her experiences in the house, I’ve read about King Phillip’s war and the soldiers buried on the property, the family burial ground where generations are sitting in the dirt next to the house.”Lux’s experienceLux, on her Instagram, writes that she was initially very excited to stay inside the house. She writes,“Two years ago, we stayed inside the Conjuring House. I love ghost stories and I was looking forward to having some type of experience to confirm that there is something else out there…”But she had no ‘visibly ghostly’ experience. She writes, “No door slammed, nothing flew at us, no ghosts appeared. But, I never expected a house/land to feel so “sick”. Going into the house in high spirits, we all very quickly felt so off, anxious, and uncomfortable.”However, there was some different feeling inside the house which certainly was not the happy one. Because on the next picture slide, she explains this weird feeling:“The air feels thick. The house was freezing cold when the temperature outside wasn’t. There were foul smells that would come and go. I felt brave walking into this house but after an hour I had no interest in walking anywhere alone, no matter where you walked you didn’t feel alone.”Different from a conventional horror attractionAnd that feeling is exactly what makes the Conjuring House different from a conventional haunted attraction. It is not a studio-built haunted mansion designed for Halloween. The farmhouse has seen several families, witnessed generations and remained standing long before the movie turned its story into a global horror franchise.For paranormal enthusiasts, this authenticity has turned the property into something of a bucket-list destination. Since it was opened to visitors in 2019, the house has at different times hosted history tours and overnight experiences.However, for now, the house is not open for public viewing or overnight experience because of some repair works.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sagrada Familia, world's tallest church, got a 24-tonne ‘glue job’ to stand tall ahead of its architect's centenary
articles.summary: Europe News: A Spanish glue company's bonds played an essential role in the binding of stone and steel for the Sagrada Familia temple's 826 panels. The world's tal.
articles.body: A Spanish glue company's bonds played an essential role in the binding of stone and steel for the Sagrada Familia temple's 826 panels. The world's tallest church, which was blessed by Pope Leo XVI last week, had been a century in the making. Its architect Antoni Gaudi knew exactly what the six central towers should look like, but what he did not know was that technology would play a pivotal role in the realisation of his dreams.Located in the heart of Barcelona, the monument is one of the architect's many masterpieces. His unique interpretation of Christianity, nature, geometry and the world produced a complex design that is innovative to date.From sandstone to a modern construction systemThe first stone for the construction was laid in 1882 under the direction of Francisco de Paula del Villar. A year later, it was reinterpreted by Gaudí to become a Barcelona landmark and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Gaudí began the Sagrada Família with the crypt and the apse wall, employing traditional methods: small stones and manual adjustments by stonemasons. However, in the final stage of his life, while working on the Nativity Façade, he introduced innovative materials for the time, including concrete in the upper sections, and utilised prefabricated elements.Initially, Gaudí used sandstone from Barcelona’s Montjuïc mountain. Highly prized by architects, this sedimentary rock stands out for its superior strength compared to other varieties and for its wide range of colours: light grey, greenish grey, beige, yellow, ochre, gold, purple and reddish tones. However, when construction of the Passion Façade began, the shortage of Montjuïc stone became evident.Gaudí died in 1926, leaving only partial models and conceptual designs for the unfinished basilica, meaning subsequent architects had to interpret his complex geometric intentions. Shortly afterwards, quarrying was abruptly and permanently halted. Since then, its construction and logistics operations have continued to evolve.A project in motionWhat Gaudí had planned by hand was ultimately completed by machines. “Technologies have revolutionised our processes. In many cases, they’ve brought to life ideas that Gaudí had already envisioned or begun,” said David Puig, Assistant Architect.One of the hallmarks of his method is that the interior geometries evoke shapes found in nature: straight lines are arranged to create the illusion of undulating columns and walls. “To carry out such a complex geometric project, two-dimensional plans weren’t enough for Gaudí; he needed to work in three dimensions using plaster models.” Today, digital modelling through CAD and BIM programs, specialised in architectural design and 3D simulation, has simplified both the design and execution of the project.Since the same array of colours could not be found in present-day Barcelona, stones from Germany, France and UK were delivered for construction through an international logistics network. The scale of the project, limited space on the site, increasingly occupied by the construction itself, and the constant flow of visitors led the Construction Board to implement its own logistical system.The solution was to move much of the work off-site: elements are prefabricated in external workshops and only transported to the basilica for final assembly. This was the case, for example, with singular pieces like the star atop the Virgin Mary Tower and the cross that will crown the Jesus Christ Tower; these works were crafted in specialised facilities before being transported and assembled in Barcelona.Glued together, literallyBut what still remains one of the most interesting parts about the project is its use of glue. Specifically, Loctite EA 9497 from Henkel, the element that has made it possible for stone and steel to behave as a single material.According to a report by Euronews, the towers have been built using a modular system of prestressed stone panels, 826 in total, incorporating more than 2,100 stone elements joined to metal structures. Each panel required around 30 kilos of adhesive. In all, 24 tonnes were applied in liquid form, able to fill every cavity and secure the joint before a curing process of around 24 hours began. The bond withstands loads equivalent to 100,000 people per square metre or the weight of 1,600 African elephants.A figure that explains why the Tower of Jesus Christ, the tallest in the complex, can support the large cross that crowns it without compromising a single millimetre of stability.Why the glue mattersThe glue matters because the surroundings matter. The basilica is just over two kilometres from the Mediterranean, exposed to constant salinity and a permanent risk of corrosion. And underground, two metro lines send constant vibrations through the entire structure. These pose constant challenges to the sanctity of the ongoing construction.The collaboration between Henkel and the Sagrada Familia goes back a long way. The relationship has lasted more than a decade, with tests exceeding usual standards and a logistics supply chain that has had to adapt to something rare in the construction world: a project funded solely by visitors’ contributions, with no fixed timetable or final budget.At 172.5 metres, the Sagrada Familia is now the tallest religious temple in the world, ahead of Ulm Minster in Germany. “This project highlights how innovation and collaboration continue to drive progress,” said Adrián Orbea, president of Henkel Ibérica.“We have around a hundred professionals dedicated to three main areas: the architectural project, construction and basilica management. This is complemented by collaborations with external companies,” said Puig. For years, 2026 was cited as the symbolic completion date, coinciding with the 100th anniversary of Gaudí’s death. As of now, its central tower has been completed this year, but the overall basilica still remains unfinished.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: CJP protest assault case: 'Influencer' Swatantra Bhardwaj gets 3-week interim bail
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Tuesday granted Swatantra Bhardwaj interim bail for three weeks in connection with the alleged assault of the father of a .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Tuesday granted Swatantra Bhardwaj interim bail for three weeks in connection with the alleged assault of the father of a Dalit student-activist during a protest at Jantar Mantar.Bhardwaj is facing charges in connection with the alleged assault during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar in June. He was arrested in Uttar Pradesh on September 5 and has been in judicial custody.The court's interim bail order comes a day after Bhardwaj's counsel argued that his arrest was politically motivated and claimed that the complainant had attacked Bhardwaj during the incident.During Monday's hearing, advocate Umesh Sharma told the court that a video purportedly showed the complainant attacking Bhardwaj."Police ko wo video nazar nahi aa raha... Is video m clearly dikhai de raha hai ki complainant is mujhpe attack kiya hai aur main gir gaya hu (The police are not able to see that video. It is clearly visible in this video that the complainant attacked me and I fell down)," Sharma told the court.Sharma also alleged that Bhardwaj was arrested under the SC/ST Act for political reasons. He said Bhardwaj had initially received a police notice to appear for questioning on June 27 and appeared before investigators on June 29, after which he was allowed to leave."The police issued me a notice on June 27 to appear for questioning, and I appeared for questioning on June 29. After that, I was allowed to go. Then, after some political developments, I was arrested on September 4. After my arrest, a new FIR [under POCSO] was registered," Sharma said.Advocate Swati Khanna, appearing for the complainant, opposed the bail plea and alleged that Bhardwaj had used casteist slurs against the complainant. She also claimed that Bhardwaj had admitted in a video that he was the one who attacked the complainant.Delhi Police told the court that the original complaint did not mention any casteist slur. However, a casteist slur was included in a subsequent statement, following which provisions of the SC/ST Act were added.Khanna also informed the court that Bhardwaj had approached the Delhi high court with a habeas corpus plea challenging his arrest, but the plea was rejected.Bhardwaj was initially booked under Sections 115(2) and 126(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), relating to causing simple hurt and wrongful restraint. The case was later expanded to include provisions of the SC/ST Act and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO).Delhi Police had earlier extended Bhardwaj's judicial custody until September 21. The action followed protests by CJP leaders, the student and her father outside the Parliament Street police station demanding his arrest.Bhardwaj had also claimed in an interview that he had “cracked the skull” of the girl's father during the protest and escaped arrest because of his political connections. He had claimed proximity to NDA leaders Kapil Mishra and Chirag Paswan, though Paswan denied the claim and filed a separate complaint against him for allegedly misusing his name.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Number of centenarians in Japan passes 100,000 for first time
articles.summary: The number of centenarians in Japan has for the first time exceeded 100,000, the Health Ministry in Tokyo said on Tuesday. A total of 107,677 people aged 100...
articles.body:
The number of centenarians in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, with 107,677 people aged 100 or over now living in the country.

Japan has seen a continuous increase in the number of centenarians for 56 consecutive years, with only 153 centenarians in 1963 compared to over 100,000 today.

Despite the high life expectancy in Japan, the country's population is shrinking rapidly due to low birth rates and immigration levels, leading to rising social security costs and a significant national debt.

The number of centenarians in Japan has for the first time exceeded 100,000, the Health Ministry in Tokyo said on Tuesday.

A total of 107,677 people aged 100 or over now live in the world's fourth-largest economy - 7,914 more than a year earlier.

"We are pleased that many people are living longer and remaining active thanks to advances in medical technology," Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno told reporters.

The number of centenarians has risen every year for 56 consecutive years. When Japan began keeping statistics in 1963, the island nation counted just 153 centenarians. Twenty-five years later the figure had already exceeded 10,000.

According to the latest survey, around 88% of all centenarians are women. Japan has one of the highest life expectancies in the world, with women living to around 87 and men to around 81.

At the same time, Japan's population is shrinking at a record pace due to low birth rates and comparatively low levels of immigration. At the start of the year, the number of Japanese citizens fell below 120 million for the first time in 42 years, to around 119.7 million. Within a single year, the country's population shrank by 917,000 - roughly the size of a large city.

The costs of social security in Japan are rising year on year due to the declining birth rate and the ageing population, placing an increasing burden on public finances. This is happening in a country that already has by far the highest level of national debt among industrialized nations.

articles.title: In 2008, actor Josh Duhamel bought 12 acres with a rustic fixer-upper cabin in Minnesota, with no electricity or running water, then expanded to 52 acres; now he has built an off-grid family retreat
articles.summary: News News: When he is not swamped with his Hollywood projects, Josh Duhamel retreats to his off-grid property in Minnesota, where outdoor barbecues, fishing and .
articles.body: When he is not swamped with his Hollywood projects, Josh Duhamel retreats to his off-grid property in Minnesota, where outdoor barbecues, fishing and lake days offer him and his son a taste of the simple life.Duhamel bought his first parcel of Minnesota lakefront land around 2008. Soon enough, he purchased the property next to it, bringing the total to 52 acres. The land sat empty except for an old cabin. It was the kind of fixer-upper that most buyers avoid. The cabin had no electricity or plumbing. For most people, it would be a cautionary tale. For Duhamel, it became the most meaningful investment he had ever made. The land was in the woods near a lake, an hour-plus drive from Fargo and his home state of North Dakota. The property sits 40 minutes from civilisation in northwest Minnesota, nestled on a lake not far from where his father lives. So, for him, buying this land only made sense. The fixer-upper soon became his favourite getaway spot. Now with all the amenities, the Minnesota cabin is every bit the family retreat he dreamt of.A perfect getawayBefore becoming the heartthrob of Hollywood, Josh Duhamel was an outdoorsy guy. As a kid, he chased salamanders in the woods of North Dakota. "My buddies and I were living our lives like Huck Finn," the actor, 53, told Men’s Journal. His days were spent fishing in the summer and sledding in the winter. Those memories made him want a place in Minnesota’s wilderness, and that led him to purchase the fixer-upper cabin."My father lives in Minnesota. The place that I got is near his, on the lake and out in the deep woods. There is nobody around for miles. I always come back with my spirit feeling lifted," he told the outlet.When he bought the property, it was just a piece of land with a cabin on it. "It was just half a parcel of land at first, which had an old cabin on it with no plumbing or electricity," he said. But he had no complaints. In fact, he found the place refreshing. Going back to a simple life only brought him joy. "Straight-up old-fashioned outhouse, and it was time to shower in the lake. There is something special about going back to the basics, and having that solitude."Building from scratchWhile the wilderness of Minnesota and the fun the lake and outdoors had to offer were exhilarating, the challenges inside the cabin were real. The initial cabin offered nothing but the basics. Water came from the lake. Waste went into an outhouse. The first years were genuinely rustic. Showers meant a trip to the lake. Doing dishes involved carrying water. It wasn’t glamorous, but it was real.When the neighbouring property came on the market, the actor bought it, taking the whole property to 52 acres. That second parcel had electricity. Over time, a third parcel joined the portfolio, bringing with it another structure. The transition from outhouse to infrastructure took time. Digging a well became a priority once he could afford it. ‘I put in a well this year, so we finally have a working toilet and shower inside,’ he told the outlet during their 2017 interview. Running water meant no more shuttling to the lake. Electricity from the second cabin followed. With power and water secured, he could focus on other improvements: a boat dock for fishing, cleared areas for grilling, and the kind of installations that transform raw land into liveable space.His days at the cabin are pretty much unplanned. He would do everything: chop wood, go fishing and prep the barbecue. ‘I got a Toolcat, a Bobcat machine that has a digger and a grabber. So I will jump on that and literally just tool around all day. Then when it’s time for dinner, we’ll get the fire pit going and grill something up,’ the actor said. It’s the kind of life he expected from the place. For leisure, he goes swimming. ‘Oh man, there is great fishing in the lake. There is plenty of walleye and trout, which taste amazing when you cook them up. Now we have a boat too,’ he said.What started as a personal escape has become a genuine family retreat. His son spends time here. The property now hosts fire pits for grilling, boats for fishing walleye and trout, and wide-open space for the kind of childhood adventures Duhamel valued while growing up in North Dakota.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Queen Elizabeth’s childhood drawings were found in a suitcase under a bed decades later; the 10-year-old princess had sketched horses, a dog and people
articles.summary: UK News: For decades, a small collection of royal correspondence remained largely out of sight, packed away in a suitcase beneath a bed. Among the papers was a.
articles.body: For decades, a small collection of royal correspondence remained largely out of sight, packed away in a suitcase beneath a bed. Among the papers was a handwritten note from Princess Elizabeth, written when she was still a child, with pencil drawings scattered across the page. The sketches show horses, people, a dog and scenes involving riding, offering a glimpse of the interests that surrounded her early years. The material was kept by the family of Beatrice Stillman, a former head housemaid at Royal Lodge. According to the BBC, it was only discovered again in 2024, after the suitcase was found among belongings left in the family home.Princess Elizabeth’s letter captures her childhood at Royal LodgeThe letter dates from the period between 1936 and 1940, when Princess Elizabeth was still a child. She was around 10 when Beatrice Stillman joined the household at Royal Lodge, although auctioneers cannot establish the precise date on which the note was written.At the time, the royal family regularly spent periods away from their Windsor home. The letter was written from Praa Sands in Cornwall, where Elizabeth described being able to reach the beach directly from the garden. Her attention, however, was not limited to the holiday itself.She asked whether the birds were well and whether the goldfish had survived in her absence. She also mentioned Jock, one of the ponies associated with her childhood, saying that he was well and happy.There was a practical kindness in another part of the note. Elizabeth had picked wild primroses and wanted some given to other members of the Royal Lodge household. The flowers were to be shared with Miss Coote and Mrs Wade.For a young princess writing to a member of staff, it was a small exchange. It also provides an unusually personal record of the people and animals occupying her thoughts at the time.Childhood sketches reveal Elizabeth’s love of animalsThe most distinctive part of the material is the collection of drawings made around the correspondence. They include two horses and highwaymen, a seated girl identified as Mary, a dog named Jim and a boy called John, according to Hansons Auctioneers. There is also a scene showing a boy and a pony jumping over a five-bar gate. Another drawing shows a man beside a horse, apparently patting it.The sketches are informal rather than finished illustrations. They have the quality of things drawn for amusement, with names and subjects added around the figures. Together, they give a picture of a child whose interests included animals, riding and people around her. Elizabeth's later affection for horses and dogs is well documented, but these early drawings place those interests much further back in her life.The letter also mentions Jock, one of the ponies from her childhood. Author Gyles Brandreth has written about Elizabeth's ponies, including Jock and Hans, adding context to the otherwise brief reference in the note.The royal household notes preserved by Beatrice’s familyThe recipient, Beatrice Stillman, became head housemaid at Royal Lodge in 1936. Her work placed her within the domestic life of the royal household, and she appears to have formed a familiar relationship with the young princesses.The archive discovered by her family contains more than Elizabeth's letter. It also includes correspondence from the palace and other pieces of paper connected with the royal household.One particularly short note came from Princess Margaret. Written in pencil, it simply asked Beatrice to look after her bathing suit.The contrast between the two surviving notes is striking without needing much interpretation. Elizabeth's message is concerned with flowers, animals and other members of the household, while Margaret's is a child's practical request about something she wanted kept safe. Both girls were still very young when the papers were written.Royal letters rediscovered in a family suitcaseThe documents remained in the family after Beatrice's death. A suitcase containing the letters, Christmas cards and other material eventually passed to Jean Westacott, Beatrice's niece. After Jean died, her son William Westacott and other family members came across the suitcase in 2024. It had been sitting under her bed.The family already knew that the letters existed, but seeing the original papers was different from knowing about them. Westacott, who lives in Sevenoaks, said, "We knew the letters existed, but to read them in the flesh was a 'wow' moment." The archive had effectively survived without being treated as a major historical collection. It was family material, kept and passed down, until its contents were examined more closely.Beatrice’s connection with the royal family continuedStillman's relationship with the royal household did not end with her employment at Royal Lodge. She later married Alfred Twyman, a gardener working on the Windsor estate, in 1946. The surviving material also reflects a connection between the Stillman family and the royal household during the Second World War.Beatrice's brother-in-law, John Dicker, was killed during an air raid in 1940. After his death, the Queen Mother invited his widow, who was Beatrice's sister, and their two young daughters, Rene and Jean, to Royal Lodge to spend time with Elizabeth and Margaret.Rene, now 95, later remembered meeting George VI, the Queen and the two princesses. She also recalled playing in the large playhouse in the Royal Lodge garden.The wartime circumstances added another layer to the relationship. According to the family, the Queen gave some of the princesses' clothes to the children at a time when resources were being stretched by the conflict.Royal Lodge was part of Elizabeth’s childhoodRoyal Lodge had been given to the royal family by George V in 1931 as a weekend retreat. The house stood around three miles south of Windsor Castle and became closely associated with the childhood years of Elizabeth and Margaret.Its grounds included Y Bwthyn Bach, the miniature cottage presented to Elizabeth by the people of Wales in 1932. The young princesses also had space there for outdoor play and time away from the more formal surroundings of the royal household.The Cornwall letter belongs to this period, before the war altered the girls' routines. In May 1940, Elizabeth and Margaret moved to Windsor Castle for their safety. That provides a useful boundary for dating the document. Beatrice had joined the household in 1936, while the princesses' move to Windsor in 1940 means the letter must have been written within those years.The auction brings a private royal childhood to lightThe papers do not document a major royal event. There is no speech, official ceremony or political episode attached to them. Instead, they preserve a few mundane details. A child was away on holiday, wondering about the animals left behind. She had picked primroses and wanted other people to enjoy them. Around the letter were pencil sketches of horses, children and a dog.That is part of what makes the archive useful as a historical record. Royal childhood is often remembered through photographs, public appearances and carefully recorded occasions. A handwritten note kept by a household employee belongs to a much less formal part of that life.The letter is now being offered at auction by Hansons Auctioneers at its Penshurst saleroom in Kent. It carries an estimate of £2,000 to £4,000, with the sale scheduled for 27 February 2026. For the family that kept the papers, their significance only became clear when the suitcase was finally opened. Inside were fragments of a relationship that had begun at Royal Lodge, preserved through several generations without attracting much attention.Among them were the drawings of a future queen as a child, surrounded by the animals and people that filled her small world.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
articles.summary: The Danish prime minister has accused Russia of "reckless" behaviour, while the Kremlin is yet to comment.
articles.body:
Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".

Russia said it would "thoroughly investigate" the incident but accused Danish helicopters of making "dangerous manoeuvres" near Russian warships.

It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."

Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.

The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."

In a statement following the incident, Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin accused Denmark of "recklessness" and "provocative actions".

Barbin said this was "not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships". He added that the latest incident showed that "communication problems lie not with the Russian Navy's vessels, but with the Danish side".

Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no attempt to make contact with helicopters had been made by the frigate's crew.

Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.

Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.

The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months.

President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".

It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions".

Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.

Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.
